linear-regression.title: Predict before calculating
linear-regression.prompt: For points (0,2), (1,5), and (2,8), predict the fitted slope before entering a table.
linear-regression.explanation: Each one-unit x increase adds 3 to y, so all points lie on y = 3x + 2. Regression should reproduce slope 3.

linear-regression.title: Check the tool’s limits
linear-regression.prompt: Why does fitting a line to three exact collinear points not prove that a real process stays linear outside the observed inputs?
linear-regression.sampleAnswer: The fit describes these points. Extrapolation assumes the same relationship continues beyond the observations, which needs contextual evidence. A perfect in-sample fit does not establish that assumption.

sliders.title: Predict before calculating
sliders.prompt: In y = a(x−2)² + 1, which slider value produces a downward-opening parabola?
sliders.explanation: A negative coefficient reverses the vertical orientation. At a = 0 the relation is the horizontal line y = 1, not a parabola.

sliders.title: Check the tool’s limits
sliders.prompt: Explain which features remain fixed while a changes through nonzero values, and what happens at a = 0.
sliders.sampleAnswer: For nonzero a, the vertex remains (2,1) and the symmetry line remains x = 2. The sign changes opening direction and the magnitude changes vertical scale. At zero the relation becomes y = 1, so there is no unique parabola vertex.

systems.title: Predict before calculating
systems.prompt: Before graphing y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3, predict the number of intersections.
systems.explanation: The distinct lines have equal slopes and different intercepts, so they are parallel.

systems.title: Check the tool’s limits
systems.prompt: Why can a graphing window make y = x and y = 1.001x − 100 appear to have no intersection? Find the intersection algebraically.
systems.sampleAnswer: The slopes differ, so an intersection exists. Solving x = 1.001x − 100 gives x = 100000 and y = 100000. A typical window hides that location; absence from the screen is not proof of no solution.

absolute-value.title: Predict before calculating
absolute-value.prompt: How many real solutions does |x−3| = −2 have?
absolute-value.explanation: Absolute value is nonnegative for every real input; it cannot equal −2.

absolute-value.title: Check the tool’s limits
absolute-value.prompt: Explain why solving |x−3| = 2 by graphing y = x−3 and y = 2 misses a solution.
absolute-value.sampleAnswer: The absolute-value graph has two branches. The equation requires x−3 = 2 or x−3 = −2, giving x = 5 or x = 1. The single straight line represents only one branch.

inequalities.title: Predict before calculating
choices: Only if the boundary is solid
inequalities.explanation: Substitution gives 0 > −1, which is true. The strict inequality excludes the boundary itself.

inequalities.title: Check the tool’s limits
inequalities.prompt: How would replacing > with ≥ change the graph and the solution set?
inequalities.sampleAnswer: The boundary line becomes included, usually shown solid instead of dashed. Points strictly above stay included; points on y = 2x − 1 are newly included. The shaded side remains the same.

parabolas.title: Predict before calculating
parabolas.prompt: Where is the vertex of y = (x+3)² − 4?
parabolas.explanation: The squared expression is zero at x = −3, giving the minimum output −4.

parabolas.title: Check the tool’s limits
parabolas.prompt: A graph shows only one intercept of y = (x−50)² − 1. How can you find and verify both without trusting the window?
parabolas.sampleAnswer: Set the output to zero: (x−50)² = 1, so x = 49 or 51. Substitute both into the equation, then adjust the window to include them. A narrow window may hide a valid root.

circles.title: Predict before calculating
circles.explanation: The constant is the radius squared, so r² = 9 and r = 3. The center is (2,−1).

circles.title: Check the tool’s limits
circles.prompt: Explain why x² + y² = 9 can look like an ellipse on a screen, and give an algebraic check of its intercepts.
circles.sampleAnswer: Unequal visual scales on the axes can distort appearance. Setting y = 0 gives x = ±3; setting x = 0 gives y = ±3. Equal coordinate distances confirm a radius of 3, even if the screen stretches one direction.

mean-median.title: Predict before calculating
mean-median.prompt: For [1,2,3,4,100], which statistic changes more if 100 is replaced by 1000?
mean-median.explanation: The median remains 3. The sum increases by 900, so the mean rises by 900/5 = 180.

mean-median.title: Check the tool’s limits
mean-median.prompt: Why does entering a frequency table as a plain list of the distinct values give the wrong mean when frequencies differ?
mean-median.sampleAnswer: A distinct-value list gives each listed value equal weight. A frequency table requires each value to contribute according to its count. Compute the weighted sum divided by the total count, or construct the full repeated-value list.

fractions.title: Predict before calculating
fractions.explanation: Use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Adding denominators does not represent the sum.

fractions.title: Check the tool’s limits
fractions.prompt: A calculator shows 0.333333 for one third. Why should you retain 1/3 when multiplying it by 3?
fractions.sampleAnswer: The displayed decimal is rounded. Keeping the exact fraction gives 3 × (1/3) = 1, while multiplying a truncated decimal can give 0.999999. Preserve exact forms until the requested final rounding.

percents.title: Predict before calculating
percents.prompt: A quantity rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What fraction of its original value remains?
percents.explanation: Successive changes multiply: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96. The second change uses the increased base.

percents.title: Check the tool’s limits
percents.prompt: An amount after a 20% increase is 72. Why is subtracting 20% of 72 the wrong way to recover the original?
percents.sampleAnswer: The original was multiplied by 1.20, so divide 72 by 1.20 to get 60. Subtracting 20% of 72 uses a different base and gives 57.6. Reverse the multiplier instead.
